title: Ghar and rahao
hookLine: the heading ghar gives a rhythm or musical setting; rahao marks the refrain

lines: SRI RAG, MAHALA ONE, GHAR ONE.
cards: Above the first hymn of Sri Rag in the Guru Granth Sahib, the heading reads, in Gurmukhi: Sri Rag, Mahala one, Ghar one. A few syllables, three pieces of news. Sri Rag is the raga.
Mahala one says the hymn is Guru Nanak's. And ghar? In everyday Punjabi, ghar is a house, a home.
So what is a house doing at the top of a hymn, among the musical directions?

teach.b: In the headings, ghar is a musical instruction. The raga gives the notes and the mood; the ghar number tells singers something more about how to set the hymn. Exactly what, the Granth never explains, and readers differ.

teach.h: A BEAT CYCLE, OR A MELODIC SETTING?
teach.b: Some musicians and scholars hear ghar as a beat cycle, a taal, the rhythm the hymn moves in. Others hear a variant of the raga's melody, or a particular way of singing it.
What anyone can see is that the number is written onto the page: one more clue from the Gurus about how the words should sound. Inside the hymn comes a second mark. Rahao.
It means pause, or stay. It's written after one line, and that line is the refrain. Go back to that first hymn of Sri Rag, the palace of pearls you met earlier on the path.
Its rahao line says, in paraphrase: without the Lord, my soul burns to ashes; I asked my Guru, and I saw there is no other place.
In kirtan, singers often return to the rahao line between the verses, so the hymn keeps coming home to it. Some teachers put it simply: if you want the heart of a shabad, read the rahao first.
So the two marks belong together.
Ghar is the house the tune lives in. Rahao is the room in that house the singer keeps walking back into. The heading gives the address; the rahao tells you where to sit down.

how: Ragis singing a shabad commonly use its rahao line as the refrain, returning to it between the verses, and Sikh teachers point to the rahao as a key to a shabad's meaning.

games.q: you're singing a shabad for the first time and lose your place between verses. where do you go back to?
o: the first line of the hymn.
games.why: rahao means pause, or stay: it marks the refrain singers keep returning to, and some teachers call it the heart of the shabad.

practice: If you have a gutka, a printed Granth or a Granth app, open past the opening prayers and look above a hymn for the raga, the Mahala, and perhaps ghar with a number; then find rahao inside it and read the line before it slowly, two or three times.
If you have nothing to open, say today's heading softly once, Sri Rag, Mahala one, Ghar one, and let the rest of the sit be what rahao asks: stay.
If you pray, come back to Waheguru each time the mind wanders, the way a singer comes back to the refrain.

wordCard.voice: Ghar. House, home; in the Granth's headings, a musical instruction for setting the hymn, beside rahao, the pause that marks the refrain. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: house, home; in the Granth's headings, a musical instruction. Punjabi speakers say the gh with a tone; a Keeper can model it.

carryVoice: Your line: the house of the tune. Ghar is the house; rahao is the room the singer comes back to. See you tomorrow.
